ACCESS FINANCIAL SERVICES, INC.  
   January 9, 2025 
Quarterly Review and Outlook  
 Fourth Quarter, 2024
Index Returns as of Dec. 31, 2024   3 Mo.  6 Mo.  12 Mo. 
 Source: Bloomberg & Morningstar 
As was the case in 2023, US stocks as measured by the 
S&P 500 Index (SPX) had an exceptional 2024, posting 
returns of 25%. These strong returns reflect robust 
growth expectations as consumption and investment 
proved resilient to high borrowing costs. This, in turn, 
fueled ‘soft landing’ optimism, encouraging a further 
rotation towards risky assets. President Trump’s 
election further turbo charged the US stock market 
relative to foreign stocks by around 9% (vertical line 
on Chart 1) on his promise to deliver growth 
accelerating tax cuts while waging a trade war that 
should hurt foreign and help domestic producers.  
Yet much like last year, gains were highly 
concentrated, with mega-cap technology related stocks 
(the Magnificent 71 in particular) outpacing the rest of 
the market (Chart 2). According to FactSet Research, 
2024 earnings growth for the Magnificent 7 was 33% 
while earnings growth for the remaining 493 companies 
was just 4%. Aside from macro optimism, technology 
related companies are benefiting from artificial 
intelligence (AI) adoption and rapid growth in software 
investment.  
1 NVIDIA, Meta (Facebook), Tesla, Amazon, Alphabet (Google), 
Apple and Microsoft 
Investors’ love affair with technology related stocks 
resulted in large gaps in performance across factors: 
growth stocks more than doubled value stocks, cyclical 
stocks tripled defensives, and large cap stocks 
outperformed small cap stocks by 13%.

services fueled SPX earnings, foreign markets faced

limited technology stock exposure, and a string of 
political crises. Emerging market stocks fared better, 
but still faced pressure from US dollar strength and 
weak growth in China. 
 
Bonds, too, have continued to struggle, posting weaker 
returns than in 2023 despite the Federal Open Market 
Committee (the ‘Fed’) cutting the federal funds rate by 
1% (Chart 3). 
 
Chart 3: Federal Funds Rate 
 
 
Chart source: Access Financial Services using Bloomberg Software & Data 
 
A key drag on bond returns has been the significant 
reversal in market expectations for the change in the 
federal funds rate since September. Expectations have 
moved from aggressive cuts (nine quarter point cuts 
over the next year at the end of last quarter) to 
‘higher-for-longer’ (between one and two rate cuts 
over the next year) (Chart 4). More recently, Trump’s 
win lifted longer term interest rates by renewing 
inflation worries. 
 
Chart 4: Change in Fed Funds Rate cut Expectations 
 
 
Chart source: Access Financial Services using Bloomberg Software & Data 
 
The Fed embarked on a rate cutting cycle despite an 
absence of lasting economic or market distress: 
> 
Stocks are near all-time highs 
> 
Indications are for a cyclical upturn in US growth 
> 
Near-term recession risk is low 
> 
Inflation is sticky and price pressures are building 
> 
Real household incomes are rising despite higher 
rates and corporations look in good shape 
This loosening makes more sense in the context of the 
government’s rising interest bill though. 
 
The increasing interest liability has the potential – if 
allowed to continue unchecked – to lead to a fiscal or 
political crisis. The liability stands at an eye-watering 
$1.1 trillion annually. This is about 22% of total 
government revenue versus an average of 14.8% 
between 2000 and 2022 (Chart 5). Interest payments 
now exceed national defense, Medicare and Medicaid. 
 
Chart 5: US Government Interest Payments as Percentage 
of Total Receipts 
 
 
Chart source: Access Financial Services using Bloomberg Software & Data 
 
Longer term bond yields lead the Treasury’s total 
interest expense by about six months and have been 
rising. While the Fed doesn’t directly set longer term 
yields, it hopes to influence them through the rate-
expectations channel and its inflation fighting 
credentials. 
 
Returning to the US stock market, split by source, this 
year’s stock market strength reflects strong earnings 
growth from technology related companies and 
valuation expansion to levels rarely seen (Chart 6) - 
levels that have preceded market declines in the past. 
In the case of earnings, the US stock market clearly 
benefited from its high technology stock weighting as 
spending on technology far outpaced demand for other 
goods and services. As for valuations, higher multiples 
reflect risk taking in response to soft landing optimism 
and strong expected earnings growth going forward. 
 
Wall Street analysts expect this upswing to continue 
predicting a double digit increase in SPX in 2025 (Table 
1). Underscoring this bullish view are expectations for 
very strong earnings growth, further AI investments, 
Fed easing, and tax cuts by the incoming administration 
this year. 
 
2

 
Chart 6: S&P 500 Valuation Measures 
 
 
Chart source: Access Financial Services using Bloomberg Software & Data 
 
It is interesting to note that analysts believe earnings 
growth for companies outside the Magnificent 7 will 
improve meaningfully in 2025. While they expect the 
Magnificent 7 companies to report earnings growth of 
21% in 2025, they expect the other 493 companies to 
report earnings growth of 13% for 2025 versus the 4% 
in 2024. 
 
We also expect corporate earnings to grow this year, 
just not to the degree analysts are predicting. Stock 
market forecasters in aggregate have never predicted 
a down year for the SPX over the last 25 years. I guess 
no one ever got sacked for predicting the market will 
go up. 
 
With the top ten stocks in the SPX now accounting for 
around 40% of the index’s market capitalization (Chart 
7 & 8), and all but two of them (Berkshire Hathaway 
and JPMorgan Chase) being technology related 
companies, the market’s returns going forward are 
heavily dependent on continued strong earnings growth 
from these few companies that have driven the stock 
market higher over the last two years. 
 
Individual investors are no less bullish than 
professional forecasters. US households are now as 
invested in stocks as they ever have been, with data 
going back to the 1940s. The household sector’s stock 
ownership is now at 43% of financial assets, exceeding 
the high reached in 2021 (Chart 9). And, it is not just 
households, the cross-sector (households, corporates, 
financials and foreigners) ownership of equities also 
hit an all-time high compared to financial assets held. 
Never before has ownership been so high with 
valuations so stretched.  
 
Table 1: Macro Strategists’ 2025 Year End S&P 500 Targets 
 
 
 
 
Table Source: Access Financial Services using data from Bloomberg 
Chart Source: Bloomberg 
 
This is not just a retail investor phenomenon. Bank of 
America’s Global Fund Manager Survey shows an 11 
year high in the net percentage of managers who say 
they are overweight US equities. 
 
While monetary and fiscal policy changes are getting a 
lot of credit as the likely drivers steering stocks into 
2025, there is a pretty long checklist of fundamental 
concerns to watch. These risks include the high 
earnings expectations embedded in stock prices, 
valuation extremes in technology related shares that 
are elevated almost any way you look at it, and the 
inconsistent history of stock prices in a president's first 
year.

The first year of a new presidency is historically 
volatile. The SPX returned between 5-10% only twice in 
the year after elections since 1953, with more 
significant gains or losses much more common. Since 
1952, a change in the White House party has also 
resulted in extremes more often than average returns. 
The last three times (2009, 2017, 2021), the S&P rallied 
hard, but was previously prone to declines on party 
change, dropping 10%-plus in three other instances. 
 
The market will have to repeat a 2017 anomaly and 
buck history to get a positive return in 2025. Only once 
since 1952, when a Republican took office from a 
Democrat, did the SPX rise the following year - and that 
was Trump in 2016. 
 
Expected earnings growth may be an impediment for 
stocks for the first year since 2022 as companies have 
been able to beat very low earnings expectations 
implied in SPX prices for the last two years. In 2023, 
the SPX's earnings per share (EPS) fell short of 
consensus at the start of the year and were close to 
what the macro outlook implied. According to 
Bloomberg Intelligence, earnings are on track to nearly 
match the bottom up forecast for 2024 but are well 
above the 2.2% implied by economic projections as well 
as what their model suggested was priced by the 
market at the beginning of the year (0.8%). 
 
The model now implies investors are expecting a 20% 
plus gain in 2025 (Table 2), so exceeding market 
implied earnings expectations looks unlikely this time 
around. 
 
Table 2: Earnings Per Share Growth by Year* 
 
* Using Consensus Estimates for 4Q 24 
Table Source: Bloomberg Intelligence 
 
The SPX’s EPS growth has exceeded 20% only three 
times in the last 20 years. Two of those instances came 
just after major recessions in 2010 and 2021, as the 
index's earnings surged after following these recession 
years. No such drawdown in earnings occurred in 2024, 
and comparables will be much harder for 2025. 
 
Tax reform also helped spark a 23% recovery in index 
EPS in 2018. However, even if tax reform is passed as 
proposed, it may effectively only reduce the tax burden 
on the SPX by about half as much as the 2017 package.  
 
Technology related stocks trade 23% above their most 
recent five year average premium to the SPX. This 
poses a risk to the overall SPX this year thanks to their 
heavy weight in the index. 
 
The SPX technology sector's market capitalization is 
also well north of its share of index earnings (Chart 
10). Currently, the technology sector makes up 31.4% of 
the SPX's market capitalization, its largest share going 
back to at least 2013. Conversely, the sector's share of

That 9.4% point gap between trailing four-quarter net 
income share and market cap share (using consensus 
estimate 4Q24 earnings) is a bit below the 11.1% high 
point from 2Q24 but well above the 1% gap average 
back to 2013. To get to average, tech's earnings share 
would have to grow to 30%. 
 
On October 15, speaking at the Economic Club of 
Chicago, Donald Trump called tariffs “the most 
beautiful word in the dictionary.” Later, he put those 
words into action by threatening a 25% tariff on all 
imports from Canada and Mexico, and an additional 10% 
tariff on Chinese imports. Collectively, the three 
countries account for 45% of US imports. 
 
Most investors think Trump is bluffing – that he will 
back down as soon as he receives some concessions. It 
is probably not quite so simple. For Trump, tariffs are 
not a means to an end, they are an end in itself. He 
wants to erect a protectionist wall around the US 
because he really does believe that other economies 
are ripping off America. Plus, he needs the money as 
interest payments on US government debt are soaring. 
 
There are a number of implications for the US economy 
as a result of a trade war. 
> 
Higher tariffs would raise import prices, depressing 
real household disposable income in the process. It 
is true that Trump does not think this will happen, 
but it is what the evidence says. For example, in 
early 2018 the Trump administration hiked tariffs 
on washing machines. Not only did the price of 
imported washing machines rise in response to the 
tariffs, but prices of domestically produced washing 
machines increased too. Dryer prices also went up, 
even though they were not subject to tariffs. 
> 
Higher tariffs will increase business costs. More 
than half of global trade consists of intermediate 
goods, which will be subject to higher tariffs. 
 
> 
Uncertainty over trade policy will also depress 
investment spending. According to the IMF, more 
than half of the damage to global growth from 
tariffs will stem from firms deciding to sit on their 
hands while they determine the fallout from the 
trade war. Higher business uncertainty is one 
reason why manufacturing construction failed to 
rise during Trump’s first term in office, despite 
lower corporate taxes. 
 
> 
By curbing demand for imports, higher tariffs will 
push up the value of the US dollar. A stronger 
dollar, in turn, will limit exports and reduce the 
dollar value of overseas revenues. A standard rule 
of thumb is that every 1% appreciation in the trade-
weighted dollar lowers S&P 500 EPS by 0.25%. The 
trade-weighted dollar has strengthened by 3.8% 
since the election and 6.9% since late September 
(Chart 11). 
Chart 11: Trade Weighted Nominal Broad Dollar Index 
 
Chart source: AFS using Bloomberg Software & Data 
> 
Tariff induced inflation could force the Fed to curtail 
the pace of rate cuts and possibly even raise rates. 
Having been badly burned by the “transitory” 
narrative three years ago, the Fed might be 
reluctant to label the inflationary consequences of 
tariffs as transitory again.  
Inflation has dominated the post-pandemic landscape 
with obvious political consequences. Incumbents have 
lost elections globally. In the US election, inflation 
consistently ranked as the main political issue in 2024 
(Chart 12). 
 
By waging a protracted and expensive trade war, 
President Trump would essentially be prioritizing the 
least relevant political issue (trade) and risk 
threatening his handling of the most relevant political 
issue (inflation), as well as the unanimously important 
issue of broad economic growth. That is a recipe for 
losing his hard-earned political capital. 
5

 
Chart 12: What is the Most Important Issue in 2024? 
 
 
Source: Access Financial Services Using Data from Cato Institute 2024 
Globalization & Trade Survey 
 
Aside from political constraints given the Republican’s 
thin majority in congress, Trump faces mathematical 
and macro constraints. Imposing a 10% tariff on the 
rest of the world would not raise sufficient revenue to 
pay for various fiscal priorities. Estimates from various 
models and scenarios put expected revenue in the $1.7 
trillion to $3 trillion range over the next decade. Even 
the optimistic figures fall well short of Trump’s 
revenue promises. 
 
Trade is a dynamic concept. And trade in the twenty-
first century is highly dynamic. We are not living in the 
nineteenth century. A tariffed trade partner does not 
have to put up with tariffs as they would have in the 
past. Today, supply chains can be reorganized and 
rebuilt rather quickly. For example, look how fast 
Ukraine managed to shift its wheat exports from the 
Black to the Baltic Sea. Or how quickly global supply 
chains adjusted to the pandemic. 
 
Many believe mathematics do not matter and that the 
Trump administration – along with its allies in 
Congress – will just ram rotten math through the 
legislative process. I am not convinced of this view as 
President Trump has a narrow majority and many 
Representatives are more than capable of doing simple 
(and complex) mathematics. 
 
But there is a broader concern for the White House. 
While they may fool the Senate politician and get a 
reconciliation bill laden with tariff “revenue” through 
Congress, they will not be able to do the same with the 
bond market and interest rates will continue rising. 
Plus, why would Trump want to put tariffs into a 
reconciliation bill making it impossible to lift tariffs in 
the future. Putting them into a legislative act would 
force him to cede power back to congress – something 
he is not a fan of. 
 
China understands the predicament that American 
policymakers have been put it in. If Trump imposed 
60% tariffs on Chinese exports, it will just direct its 
investment and capital expenditures into other nations 
to avoid the tariffs. The impact on tariff revenue to the 
US would be dramatic. If we know this, the bond market 
knows it too. As I said last quarter, it would not be 
practical to play whack-a-mole trying to tariff any 
economy that dares to host parts of the Chinese supply 
chain. 
 
Another constraint on President Trump is a macro one. 
Nobody in America really wants to work on an assembly 
line. Sure, retired union workers may talk of the good 
old days of making $40 an hour, but they are… mostly 
retired. Today, the US has only 8% of its labor force 
engaged in manufacturing (Chart 13). It is hard to 
imagine a massive shifting of supply chains to the US. 
 
Chart 13: Manufacturing Payrolls % of Labor Force 
 
 
Chart source: Access Financial Services using Bloomberg Software & Data 
 
Globally, businesses aren’t waiting until Inauguration 
Day to see which countries, products or tariff rates are 
announced. To get ahead of the game, firms are 
frontloading orders, seeking new suppliers and 
renegotiating terms with existing ones. All of this 
comes with higher costs in the form of larger 
inventories, costlier expedited shipping, or taking a 
chance on untested partners. 
 
This activity is showing up in higher frequency data. 
China’s ports saw double-digit growth in container 
throughput in the two weeks around the election and 
that rose further to an almost 30% gain in the second 
week of December. International air freight flights have 
increased by at least a third each week since mid-
October according to Bloomberg. 
 
Front running imports is a strong macro force, but when 
restocking is driven by exogenous factors instead of 
organic demand, the result is usually an inventory glut 
of unsold products. 
 
Trump is a skilled negotiator who understands game 
theory and will come out swinging. He is seemingly one 
of a very few politicians who understands the need to 
be a credible threat to one’s opponents – something the 
collective ‘west’ has not been for a very long time. He 
knows that if tariffs are to be used as a negotiation 
tool, he must convince everyone that they are not, in 
6

 
fact, a negotiating tool. The value of tariffs as leverage 
collapses if America’s economic geopolitical rivals 
perceive them as a mere negotiating tactic. Their 
utility comes if the rest of the world is convinced that 
President Trump is the “Tariff Man” who honestly 
believes that “tariff is the most beautiful word in the 
dictionary.” 
 
From my perspective, Donald Trump’s narrative is not 
what is important. Successful negotiators and 
policymakers rarely reveal their hand before 
negotiations start. What is important are the material 
constraints imposed on him by the realities of the US 
and global economy – and there are many. As time 
passes and the political and mathematical reality 
becomes apparent, I expect trade war hysteria to peak 
at some point during 2025. 
 
The boost to risk assets following Trump’s election 
persisted through early December. Since then, they 
have declined a bit while bonds have been selling off 
quite strongly (Table 3). 
 
Table 3: Returns Since December 4, 2024 
 
Source: Bloomberg 
 
Based on the bond market, it is possible that concerns 
about Trump policy-induced deficits and inflation are 
beginning to bite. Besides these concerns, bond prices 
may continue their move lower as economic growth 
persists on the back of a surge in imports as large 
restocking drives GDP growth causing the Fed’s interest 
rate cuts to be tabled (growth is inflationary and 
inflation is bad for interest rates). 
 
It is going to be difficult for risk assets to move much 
higher from here if interest rates keep rising – they 
are a material constraint to both asset prices and 
government borrowing and spending.  
 
Chart 14 shows that bond prices tend to lead stock 
prices by around four months. In order to restrain the 
rise in yields, I suspect that Trump will have to 
essentially convince the bond market that he will keep 
his fiscal priorities on the conservative side. Tariffs 
are not the answer and will fail to convince bond 
investors that tariff revenues will neutralize America’s 
worsening deficit disaster. 
 
The dangers facing risk assets are by now well known. 
They are overvalued, over-owned and over-loved, 
while liquidity is set to contract as the government 
moves from issuing Treasury Bills (short term debt) to 
longer maturities under Trump’s new Treasury 
Secretary, Scott Bessent. 
Chart 14: Bond Prices Often Lead Stock Prices 
 
 
Chart source: Access Financial Services using Bloomberg Software & Data 
 
With most investors who want to be long already long, 
valuations at very high levels, sentiment becoming 
quite exuberant (Chart 15), and animal spirits 
being roused by Trump (Chart 16), stocks are getting 
the last thing they need in one of the most widespread 
global easing cycles yet seen.

Higher This year

Granted, valuations are ignored by traders most of the 
time. They are terrible timing indicators. Elevated 
valuations just tell us that stocks are likely to have 
poor returns over the longer term, but they tell us 
nothing about how that will play out. 
 
Overall stock market volatility has been restrained by 
ultra-low individual stock correlations even though 
single stock volatility is actually quite high. The low 
correlation between individual stocks within the overall 
index results in the volatility of the index itself staying 
low. But this is an uneasy truce as correlation tends to 
rise with volatility during stock market setbacks. 
Repressed volatility, low stock correlations and 
stretched momentum have also left risk assets 
vulnerable. 
 
All the usual signs of uninhibited risk taking are there. 
When everybody is already fully invested, it becomes 
harder for prices to keep appreciating indefinitely. 
While valuations are being ignored, they are an 
indication of the elevated optimism in stock markets 
that heightens the possibility of an accident. 
 
They say you can’t run away from your past. Likewise, 
markets can’t escape from their fundamentals 
indefinitely. 
 
For now, I think the growing risk of a bond market riot 
is the greatest threat to risk assets this year. Bond 
investors are listening to Trump’s rhetoric and 
doubting the incoming administration’s ability to be 
fiscally responsible – especially given the price tag 
associated with Trump’s plans for immigration 
enforcement and sweeping tariffs. 
 
Ten year US Treasury interest rates have surged from 
3.7% in mid-September to 4.7% today. If they keep 
rising, it will be hard for risk assets to move much 
higher from here. Also, so much of the rally in risk 
assets over the last two years has been the result of 
fiscal profligacy. As/if/when fiscal conservativism 
makes a comeback, US assets are likely to take a hit. 
 
President Trump wants to leave a legacy of being a 
great president. He also sees the financial markets as 
his ultimate report card. If rising interest rates result 
in asset values declining, he will most likely temper 
his policy initiatives. 
 
For now, everyone is bullish and animal spirits are 
surging. I hope the optimism turns out to be justified 
and that the analysts and individual investors continue 
to be rewarded with outsized gains now that risk asset 
ownership is at record highs. 
 
If, on the other hand, the optimism turns out to be 
misplaced, it is going to hurt if it turns to pessimism 
and the selling begins. 
 
In general, our clients’ portfolios are underweight risk 
assets to a degree and some of the SPX exposure is 
hedged to help offset a decline in stocks should it 
happen. 
 
In the very near term, pressure on risk assets due to 
the bond market sell off seems likely to abate as bonds 
have become technically oversold implying that most of 
the selling is behind us on a short term basis. We are, 
however, anticipating more pushback from bond
